paras: The lynching of Alvin McKanna was the burning of a white lodger, known in the first reports as Miller, by a crowd of men in northern Monroe County, Mississippi, in December 1880. He was accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning to death a young farmer, his wife and their two-year-old daughter, and was killed at the scene of the fire after his capture. The case drew national wire coverage and an exchange of editorials between Northern and Southern papers over whether the burning was justice or murder.

According to a letter from Aberdeen printed in the Aberdeen Examiner, McKanna had spent a week or more in the Bigby Fork neighborhood posing as a laborer and asking for lodging at several houses. The wire versions spell the name Redding, Riding or Reding and describe two men who gave the name Miller and were allowed to sleep in the family's only room with a fireplace.

About 11 o'clock at night, on Saturday by the wire specials or Friday, December 17, by the Aberdeen letter, neighbors saw the cabin in flames and later found the charred remains of Ridings, his wife and daughter in the ruins.

Pursuers followed the two strangers, who had separated, and found the Aberdeen-bound man hiding, in a field or a pea vine pen six miles from Aberdeen by the wire accounts, or on the William B. Hogan place twelve miles from the scene by the Aberdeen letter. Brought back toward the cabin, he confessed and led his captors to the stolen goods; the Sacramento Record-Union and the Terre Haute Gazette said the confession was forced. In his reported confession, the robbers chloroformed the family, took about $27, a watch, clothes and boots, and set the bedding on fire with coal oil. The Examiner version of the confession instead blamed his accomplice for killing the couple with an axe and assaulting Mrs. Ridings before the fire.

At the burned cabin, a crowd of 25 men by the Memphis wire, or 75 by the New Orleans Times and Picayune specials, decided he should be "punished with his own weapon." They tied him to a tree or a stake, piled pine splinters around him and set him on fire. The Examiner, however, said he was "hung and burned by the citizens," and the Terre Haute Gazette said he was hanged before his body was burned.

The second man, named by the captive as John Gilmore or Gillmore, alias John Howard, was still being sought, and papers predicted he would meet the same fate. By his own reported account, given to a Tupelo Journal writer and in the Aberdeen letter, the captive was an Ohio-born escaped convict; a Terre Haute paper identified him as "Piney." No report of an inquest, arrest or trial of anyone in the crowd appears in the coverage, and the Aberdeen letter writer instead called for tramps to be arrested or put in workhouses.

Coverage came entirely from the white press, beginning with Memphis wire dispatches printed on December 21 in papers from Wheeling to Washington and Chicago. Headlines stressed the crime and called the burning retribution, as in the St. Tammany Farmer's "Speedy Retribution" and the Dallas Daily Herald's "But His Fate Is a Just One." Condensed versions garbled the place into "Tripalo" or "Tripulo" and the host into "Brown" or "Bowen."

The Sacramento Daily Record-Union rejected contemporaries who called it "a fitting punishment" and said the 25 "substantial citizens" had become murderers themselves. The National Republican mocked "a highly civilized and very Christian country" in which lynchers burned a man alive, and its own wire version was the only one to call the lodgers white. The Jackson Weekly Clarion replied that the man was an Ohioan who "deserved his fate," and later reprinted a Terre Haute Gazette editorial praising Mississippi for killing "those who shed blood." The Delaware State Journal answered the Norristown Herald's criticism of Mississippi by pointing to a lynching near Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, the same week.
The Aberdeen letter, written locally on December 21 with names and an exact date, is the most specific source, but its account of the killings rests on the captive's statement to his captors.

reader.title: Lynching of Alvin McKanna
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A party of 25 or 75 men returned a captured man accused of murder and arson to the scene and burned him to death (A1, A12, A20); the Aberdeen Examiner says he was hanged and burned by citizens (A47).

A crowd of 25 (A1, A7) or 75 (A12, A20) men killed a captured man without any legal process, to punish him 'with his own weapon' for the alleged murder of the Ridings family (A1, A20, A47). The victim is described as white (A23), which raises a scope question for an anti-Black collection but does not change the lynching definition.

Separate Tupelo specials to the Memphis papers, the Picayune and the New Orleans Times (A1, A12, A20) and an Aberdeen letter to the Examiner (A44, A47) all report the capture and killing, though they differ on details.

accounts.label: Memphis wire (Tupelo special)
accounts.gist: Two men named Miller lodged with Brown Riding on Saturday; the house burned with the family; a posse found one man in a field six miles from Aberdeen, returned him to the scene, and 25 men burned him with pine splinters.

accounts.label: Picayune and N.O. Times specials
accounts.gist: Same story with 75 men; the N.O. Times version says the captive was found in a pea vine pen and tied to a tree, and attributes the account to 'one present'; the Picayune says he was fastened to a stake.

accounts.label: Aberdeen Examiner letter ('CITIZEN')
accounts.gist: The fire was Friday, Dec. 17, at Bigby Fork; tracks led to McKanna, who was caught Saturday on the Hogan place twelve miles away, confessed, led captors to the stolen goods, and said his accomplice Gilmore used an axe; the Examiner says he was hung and burned.

accounts.label: Terre Haute Gazette
accounts.gist: Identifies the man as 'Piney', a Vigo County murderer who escaped prison, and says Mississippians forced a confession, hanged him and burned his body.

framing.detail: The Dallas Daily Herald headed the wire 'A Brute Burnt. But His Fate Is a Just One.'
The Sacramento Record-Union said the 25 'substantial citizens' became murderers themselves.
The National Republican used irony: 'a highly civilized and very Christian country' where lynchers burned a man alive.
The Jackson Weekly Clarion answered that the man was an Ohioan who 'deserved his fate'.
The Delaware State Journal rebutted the Norristown Herald's attack on Mississippi by pointing to a Pennsylvania lynching.
The Terre Haute Gazette, reprinted in the Clarion, praised Mississippi for keeping it in 'fashion to kill those who shed blood'.
Most papers ran the Memphis wire under headings like 'Horrible Tragedy', 'Judge Lynch' or 'Speedy Retribution'.

record_check.record: Five entries for Miller / unnamed man / 'brothers'
record_check.dossier: One man killed: the captive using the name Miller, who gave his name as Alvin McKanna. The second man (John Gilmore) was not caught in any report found. No fully read account calls them brothers.
Pursuit, capture, return to scene, burning; hanging only in the Examiner note and Terre Haute editorial. Property damage was the alleged crime, not the mob's act.

record_check.record: burned the Brown family after chloroforming them
record_check.dossier: Accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning Brown Ridings, his wife and daughter (family name Ridings/Redding, not Brown).
A posse captured him; a crowd of 25-75 men killed him.
The fuller wire and the N.O. Times special say the crowd 'dispensed with chloroform'; the chloroform-soaked version is a condensed variant.

info: Wire specials put the fire on Saturday night (Dec. 18) and the return and burning of the captive on the night before the Dec. 20 dispatch (Dec. 19).
A cabin in the Bigby Fork neighborhood of northern Monroe County, Mississippi, about 20 miles from Tupelo; 'Tripalo'/'Tripulo'/'Turpolo' appear only in short garbled briefs.
One man killed by the mob, a lodger who gave the name Miller; he reportedly told captors his name was Alvin McKanna, and an Indiana paper called him 'Piney'. Described as white and from Ohio.

Accused of chloroforming, robbing and burning to death Brown Ridings (Redding/Riding/Reding), his wife and two-year-old daughter; the Examiner version of his confession adds that his accomplice killed the couple with an axe and assaulted Mrs. Ridings.
A posse of neighbors captured him; a crowd of 'resolute men' burned him. No names given.
The second man was still being sought, with papers predicting he would share the same fate; no report of his capture was found.
